newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel unanimously backs Roche's Xenical.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel unanimously backs Roche's Xenical.

text.p: A panel of U.S. Food and Drug Administration advisers on Wednesday unanimously recommended approval of Roche Holding Ltd's Xenical (Orlistat Tetrahydrolipstatin) for obesity.

The panel did not make any specific suggestions about who should be prescribed the drug, but chairman Dr. Henry Bone of the Henry Ford Hospital said that he would caution against use for longer than two years.
The FDA is not bound by the panel's advice, but usually follows it.

If approved, Xenical may see U.S. sales of several hundred million dollars a year, analysts said. Xenical is not approved in any other country and has received expedited review by the FDA, according to the firm, which first applied for U.S. approval in November 1996.

The drug, which inhibits the absorption of fat, has been studied in more than 4,000 patients. According to Roche, its maximum effect is reached within a few days. Patients excrete an estimated 30 percent of fat ingested.
In trials, patients taking Xenical lost more weight and were able to keep it off longer.
According to Roche, the average patient in the one-year trials weighed 220 pounds and lost 20 pounds.

The leading obesity drug, American Home Products' Redux (Dexfenfluramine), has sold well, with 3 million prescriptions written since its launch in May 1996. But the drug is not considered ideal as it can cause a rare lung disorder in some cases and it is being investigated for potential neurotoxicity.

Knoll Pharmaceuticals, a unit of BASF AG, produced an obesity drug, Meridia (Sibutramine), that was rejected by an FDA committee in September 1996, due to concerns about its tendency to slightly increase blood pressure. This panel had no major safety concerns about Xenical.
Roche said Xenical helped reduce unhealthy side effects of obesity, by reducing cholesterol, blood pressure and insulin levels, and improving blood sugar control in diabetic patients.

Many patients experienced gastrointestinal side effects, with oily or loose stool being the primary complaint. But Roche says that these symptoms did not cause patients to drop out of trials in huge numbers.
There was a higher than expected incidence of breast cancer. Eleven patients were discovered to have tumors, but all were found within the first six months of the studies.

An independent panel evaluated the findings and concluded that in half the cases, the tumors probably already were in formation before patients began taking Xenical, and that the others most likely were due to chance. "We don't believe the findings are drug related," said Dr. Jonathan Hauptman of Roche.

FDA medical reviewer Dr. Eric Colman did not address the breast cancer finding, but when asked his opinion on the issue later, said that he "would have a great deal of trouble," making a link between the tumors and Xenical.

Xenical minimally interferes with the absorption of some fat soluble vitamins, in particular, vitamin D, E, and beta carotene. The company is recommending that patients taking Xenical be given a multivitamin supplement to offset the effect.
